records.source: Ὡς δὲ ἐκρίθη τοῦ ἀποπλεῖν ἡμᾶς εἰς τὴν Ἰταλίαν, παρεδίδουν τόν τε Παῦλον καί τινας ἑτέρους δεσμώτας ἑκατοντάρχῃ ὀνόματι Ἰουλίῳ σπείρης Σεβαστῆς.
records.gloss: When now it was decided the to sail away us to the Italy, they were handing over both the Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion by name Julius of a cohort Augustan.
pieces: Once our voyage to Italy had been decided, they placed Paul and a number of other prisoners in the custody of Julius, a centurion of the Augustan cohort.

L.1: Now when it was decided [that] we [should] sail away to Italy, they handed over both Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan cohort.

R.1: It was decided that we would sail to Italy. So Paul and some other prisoners were handed over to a centurion named Julius. A centurion was an officer over about a hundred soldiers. Julius belonged to a unit called the Augustan cohort.

decisions.choice: we: the narrator includes himself in the voyage
alternatives: the narrator only reports what others told him
decisions.reason: The first person plural, last used in 21:18, returns here and runs through the voyage to Rome (28:16). The narrator says he was on board. The sentence does not say who he is.

decisions.choice: centurion: a Roman officer over about a hundred soldiers
decisions.reason: Centurions appear often in Acts (10:1, 21:32, 22:25-26, 23:17, 24:23). Julius is answerable for the prisoners (27:42-43).

decisions.choice: the Augustan cohort: a unit bearing the honorary title of the emperor
alternatives: a unit of the emperor's personal guard in Rome
decisions.reason: Augustan was a title of honor given to several units of the Roman army. Inscriptions name a cohort with this title in Syria in the first century, but which unit Julius belonged to cannot be settled.

decisions.choice: they handed over: the officials who held Paul, after Festus's decision (25:12)
decisions.reason: The plural has no stated subject. Festus had decided to send Paul to Caesar (25:12, 25:25); his staff carry it out.

decisions.choice: A centurion was an officer over about a hundred soldiers.
decisions.reason: Readable explains the rank, as the meaning note does.

records.heading: Paul sails for Italy

records.source: ἐπιβάντες δὲ πλοίῳ Ἀδραμυττηνῷ μέλλοντι πλεῖν εἰς τοὺς κατὰ τὴν Ἀσίαν τόπους ἀνήχθημεν ὄντος σὺν ἡμῖν Ἀριστάρχου Μακεδόνος Θεσσαλονικέως·
records.gloss: Having boarded then a ship Adramyttian being about to sail to the along the Asia places, we put to sea, being with us Aristarchus a Macedonian of Thessalonica.
pieces: We went aboard a ship from Adramyttium that was due to call at ports along the coast of Asia, and we put out to sea. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.

L.2: And having boarded an Adramyttian ship about to sail to the places along [the coast of] Asia, we put to sea, Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, being with us.

R.2: We got on a ship from the town of Adramyttium. It was going to stop at ports along the coast of the province of Asia. Aristarchus came with us. He was from Thessalonica in Macedonia.

decisions.choice: Adramyttium: a port in the northwest of Asia Minor, the ship's home port
decisions.reason: The ship belonged to Adramyttium, on the coast south of Troas, and was working its way home along the coast.

decisions.choice: Asia: the Roman province in the west of Asia Minor
decisions.reason: As elsewhere in Acts (2:9, 16:6, 19:10), Asia is the province whose chief city was Ephesus.

decisions.choice: Aristarchus: Paul's companion from Thessalonica
decisions.reason: He was seized in the riot at Ephesus (19:29) and traveled with Paul to Jerusalem (20:4). Paul later calls him his fellow prisoner (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24).

decisions.choice: ports along the coast
decisions.reason: The places are harbors where a coasting ship would put in.

records.source: τῇ τε ἑτέρᾳ κατήχθημεν εἰς Σιδῶνα, φιλανθρώπως τε ὁ Ἰούλιος τῷ Παύλῳ χρησάμενος ἐπέτρεψεν πρὸς τοὺς φίλους πορευθέντι ἐπιμελείας τυχεῖν.
records.gloss: The and next [day] we put in at Sidon, kindly and the Julius the Paul having treated allowed [him], to the friends having gone, care to receive.
pieces: The next day we landed at Sidon. Julius was considerate toward Paul and allowed him to go to his friends and be looked after by them.

L.3: And on the next [day] we put in at Sidon; and Julius, treating Paul kindly, allowed [him] to go to [his] friends [and] receive care.

R.3: The next day we stopped at the city of Sidon. Julius was kind to Paul. He let Paul go to see his friends there, so that they could give him what he needed.

decisions.choice: Sidon: an old Phoenician port on the coast north of Caesarea
decisions.reason: Sidon lies on the coast of what is now Lebanon, about a day's sail north of Caesarea, where Paul had been held (23:33, 25:4).

decisions.choice: friends: very likely the believers in Sidon
alternatives: personal friends who were not believers
decisions.reason: There were believers in Phoenicia (11:19, 15:3, 21:3-7). Believers call one another friends in 3 John 15, though the word may simply mean Paul's friends.

decisions.choice: care: attention to his needs, such as food and supplies for the voyage
decisions.reason: The word means looking after someone. Prisoners on a journey often depended on friends for their needs.

decisions.choice: be looked after by them
decisions.reason: Balanced says what the care was for in natural English.

records.source: κἀκεῖθεν ἀναχθέντες ὑπεπλεύσαμεν τὴν Κύπρον διὰ τὸ τοὺς ἀνέμους εἶναι ἐναντίους, τό τε πέλαγος τὸ κατὰ τὴν Κιλικίαν καὶ Παμφυλίαν διαπλεύσαντες κατήλθομεν εἰς Μύρα τῆς Λυκίας.
records.gloss: And from there having put to sea we sailed under the Cyprus because of the the winds to be contrary, \v 5 the and sea the along the Cilicia and Pamphylia having sailed across we came down to Myra of the Lycia.
pieces: Putting out from there, we sailed on the sheltered side of Cyprus, because the winds were against us.
We crossed the open water off Cilicia and Pamphylia and came to Myra in Lycia.

L.4: And from there, having put to sea, we sailed under [the lee of] Cyprus because the winds were against [us],
L.5: and having sailed across the sea along Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came down to Myra of Lycia.

R.4: From there we sailed on. The wind was blowing against us, so we kept close to the island of Cyprus, where it gave us some shelter.
R.5: We sailed across the sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia. Then we came to the city of Myra in Lycia.

decisions.choice: sailed under Cyprus: sailed on the side of the island sheltered from the wind
alternatives: sailed below Cyprus on a map
decisions.reason: The sailing term means keeping in the lee of land. With winds from the west, the sheltered side was the east and north, between Cyprus and the mainland.

decisions.choice: contrary winds: the westerly winds of the eastern Mediterranean in summer and early autumn
decisions.reason: Ships sailing west from Syria met head winds, and so worked along the coast of Asia Minor.

decisions.choice: Myra: a port in Lycia, in the southwest of Asia Minor
decisions.reason: Myra was a harbor where ships carrying grain from Egypt to Italy put in, which is why the centurion finds one there (27:6).

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: no length of time for the crossing
decisions.reason: A few manuscripts of the Western text add that the crossing took fifteen days. The SBLGNT does not include it. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: kept close to the island of Cyprus, where it gave us some shelter
decisions.reason: Readable explains the sailing term, as the meaning note does.

records.source: κἀκεῖ εὑρὼν ὁ ἑκατοντάρχης πλοῖον Ἀλεξανδρῖνον πλέον εἰς τὴν Ἰταλίαν ἐνεβίβασεν ἡμᾶς εἰς αὐτό.
records.gloss: And there having found the centurion a ship Alexandrian sailing to the Italy, he put us into it.
pieces: At Myra the centurion came across an Alexandrian ship headed for Italy and transferred us to it.

L.6: And there the centurion, having found an Alexandrian ship sailing to Italy, put us on board it.

R.6: At Myra the centurion found a ship from Alexandria in Egypt that was sailing to Italy. He put us on that ship.

decisions.choice: an Alexandrian ship: very likely a grain ship from Egypt
decisions.reason: Egypt sent wheat to Rome by sea, and this ship carries wheat (27:38). Its size suits the 276 people on board (27:37).

decisions.choice: us: the prisoners and Paul's companions, the narrator among them
decisions.reason: The "we" of the voyage continues.

decisions.choice: At Myra; in Egypt (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the place; Readable also says where Alexandria was.

records.source: ἐν ἱκαναῖς δὲ ἡμέραις βραδυπλοοῦντες καὶ μόλις γενόμενοι κατὰ τὴν Κνίδον, μὴ προσεῶντος ἡμᾶς τοῦ ἀνέμου, ὑπεπλεύσαμεν τὴν Κρήτην κατὰ Σαλμώνην, μόλις τε παραλεγόμενοι αὐτὴν ἤλθομεν εἰς τόπον τινὰ καλούμενον Καλοὺς Λιμένας ᾧ ἐγγὺς ἦν πόλις Λασαία.
records.gloss: In many now days sailing slowly and with difficulty having come off the Cnidus, not permitting us the wind, we sailed under the Crete off Salmone, \v 8 with difficulty and coasting along it we came to a place certain being called Fair Havens, to which near was city Lasea.
pieces: For many days we made slow headway and only with difficulty arrived off Cnidus. Since the wind would not let us hold our course, we sailed in the shelter of Crete, passing Salmone.
Working our way along the shore with difficulty, we reached a place called Fair Havens, close to the town of Lasea.

L.7: And sailing slowly for many days and with difficulty coming off Cnidus, the wind not permitting us [to go on], we sailed under [the lee of] Crete off Salmone,
L.8: and coasting along it with difficulty we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near which was [the] city [of] Lasea.

R.7: For many days the ship moved slowly. It was hard work to get as far as the town of Cnidus. The wind would not let us keep going that way. So we sailed along the south side of the island of Crete, past the point of land called Salmone.
R.8: We had a hard time sailing along the coast of Crete. At last we came to a place called Fair Havens. It was near the town of Lasea.

decisions.choice: the wind did not let them go on: they could not keep their course west from Cnidus
alternatives: the wind did not let them put in at Cnidus
decisions.reason: The phrase has no object. It may mean the wind kept them from going on west, or kept them from reaching the harbor at Cnidus. Either way they turned south to Crete.

decisions.choice: Cnidus: a port at the southwest tip of Asia Minor; Salmone: a cape at the eastern end of Crete
decisions.reason: From Cnidus the ship ran south to Crete and rounded its eastern cape.

decisions.choice: Fair Havens: a small bay on the south coast of Crete, near the town of Lasea
decisions.reason: The name means good harbors. A bay on the south coast of Crete still bears the name. It gave shelter, but was not a good place to winter (27:12).

decisions.choice: along the south side of the island of Crete
decisions.reason: Readable says which side of Crete gave shelter, as the route to Fair Havens shows.

records.source: Ἱκανοῦ δὲ χρόνου διαγενομένου καὶ ὄντος ἤδη ἐπισφαλοῦς τοῦ πλοὸς διὰ τὸ καὶ τὴν νηστείαν ἤδη παρεληλυθέναι, παρῄνει ὁ Παῦλος λέγων αὐτοῖς· Ἄνδρες, θεωρῶ ὅτι μετὰ ὕβρεως καὶ πολλῆς ζημίας οὐ μόνον τοῦ φορτίου καὶ τοῦ πλοίου ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν ψυχῶν ἡμῶν μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι τὸν πλοῦν.
records.gloss: Much now time having passed and being already dangerous the voyage because of also the Fast already to have gone by, was advising the Paul \v 10 saying to them, Men, I see that with damage and much loss not only of the cargo and of the ship but also of the lives of us is going to be the voyage.
pieces: A great deal of time had gone by, and sailing was now hazardous, since even the Fast was past. So Paul gave them advice.
"Men," he said, "I can tell that this voyage is heading for harm and heavy loss, not only to the cargo and the ship but to our own lives too."

L.9: And much time having passed, and the voyage being already dangerous because even the Fast had already gone by, Paul advised [them],
L.10: saying to them, "Men, I perceive that the voyage is going to be with damage and much loss, not only of the cargo and of the ship, but also of our lives."

R.9: We had lost a lot of time. By now it was dangerous to sail, because autumn had come. The Day of Atonement, the Jewish day of fasting, was already past. So Paul warned the men in charge of the ship.
R.10: He said, "Men, I can see that this trip is going to be a disaster. We will lose the cargo and the ship, and our own lives as well."

decisions.choice: the Fast: the Day of Atonement, in late September or early October
decisions.reason: The Day of Atonement was the one fast the law of Moses commanded (Leviticus 16:29-31; 23:27). It fell on the tenth day of the seventh month. The Roman writer Vegetius says sailing was dangerous from mid-September and stopped altogether from mid-November until spring.

decisions.choice: advised: warned them, urged them to change their plan
decisions.reason: The word is used of strong advice. Paul repeats it in 27:22, when the danger has come.

decisions.choice: I perceive: Paul's own judgment of the danger
decisions.reason: Paul does not say God told him. In 27:22-24 an angel brings a new word: the ship will be lost, but no lives. His first warning was the judgment of an experienced traveler (2 Corinthians 11:25).

decisions.choice: Men: an address to the men who decided the voyage
alternatives: an address to men and women
decisions.reason: Paul speaks to the centurion, the pilot and the owner (27:11), all men.

decisions.choice: autumn had come; the Day of Atonement, the Jewish day of fasting
alternatives: the Fast had already gone by
decisions.reason: Readable says what the Fast was and why it mattered, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: the men in charge of the ship
decisions.reason: Readable names those Paul spoke to, from 27:11.

records.source: ὁ δὲ ἑκατοντάρχης τῷ κυβερνήτῃ καὶ τῷ ναυκλήρῳ μᾶλλον ἐπείθετο ἢ τοῖς ὑπὸ Παύλου λεγομένοις.
records.gloss: The but centurion by the pilot and the ship owner rather was persuaded than by the things by Paul being said.
pieces: But the centurion put more trust in the helmsman and the owner of the ship than in what Paul was saying.

L.11: But the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and the ship owner rather than by the things said by Paul.

R.11: But the centurion did not listen to Paul. Instead he listened to the man who steered the ship and to the ship's owner.

decisions.choice: pilot: the helmsman, the sailing master who steered and navigated
decisions.reason: The word means the one who steers (Revelation 18:17). He was the expert on the sea.

decisions.choice: ship owner: the owner, or the master who commanded the ship for its owners
decisions.reason: The word can mean the owner of a ship or its captain. On a grain ship working for Rome it may be the master under contract.

decisions.choice: the centurion decides: as the senior officer on board
decisions.reason: The centurion's choice settles the matter, though 27:12 says the majority agreed. Why a centurion could decide is not stated; a grain ship serving Rome may have been under his authority.

decisions.choice: helmsman
decisions.reason: In modern English a pilot is someone who guides ships into harbor or flies aircraft. Helmsman says what he did.

records.source: ἀνευθέτου δὲ τοῦ λιμένος ὑπάρχοντος πρὸς παραχειμασίαν οἱ πλείονες ἔθεντο βουλὴν ἀναχθῆναι ἐκεῖθεν, εἴ πως δύναιντο καταντήσαντες εἰς Φοίνικα παραχειμάσαι, λιμένα τῆς Κρήτης βλέποντα κατὰ λίβα καὶ κατὰ χῶρον.
records.gloss: Unsuitable now the harbor being for wintering, the majority made a plan to put to sea from there, if somehow they might be able having reached to Phoenix to winter, a harbor of the Crete looking toward southwest and toward northwest.
pieces: The harbor was a poor place to spend the winter, so most of them were for putting out to sea again, in the hope of somehow getting to Phoenix to winter there. Phoenix is a harbor in Crete that faces both southwest and northwest.

L.12: And because the harbor was unsuitable for wintering, the majority made a decision to put to sea from there, if somehow they might be able to reach Phoenix [and] winter [there], a harbor of Crete facing southwest and northwest.

R.12: The harbor at Fair Havens was not a good place to stay during the winter. So most of the men decided to sail on. They hoped they could reach Phoenix and stay there for the winter. Phoenix was a harbor on Crete that was open to the southwest and the northwest.

decisions.choice: Phoenix: a harbor farther west along the south coast of Crete
decisions.reason: The name is the same as the word for Phoenicia, but here it is a port of Crete. Its exact site is disputed.

decisions.choice: facing southwest and northwest: the directions the harbor opens toward
alternatives: facing northeast and southeast, looking down the southwest and northwest winds
decisions.reason: The Greek names two winds, the southwest wind and the northwest wind. "Looking toward" them most likely means the harbor opened in those directions. Some take it to mean it looked the way those winds blow, that is, to the east.

decisions.choice: the majority: most of those consulted, not the centurion alone
alternatives: a vote of everyone on board
decisions.reason: The decision was shared, though the centurion's view carried it (27:11).

decisions.choice: the harbor at Fair Havens
decisions.reason: Readable names the harbor, from 27:8.

records.source: Ὑποπνεύσαντος δὲ νότου δόξαντες τῆς προθέσεως κεκρατηκέναι ἄραντες ἆσσον παρελέγοντο τὴν Κρήτην.
records.gloss: Having blown gently now a south wind, having thought the purpose to have obtained, having lifted [anchor] closer they were coasting along the Crete.
pieces: When a light breeze came up from the south, they thought their plan could be carried out. So they raised anchor and sailed along Crete, close to shore.

L.13: And a south wind blowing gently, thinking they had obtained [their] purpose, having weighed [anchor], they sailed along Crete close [to shore].

R.13: Then a light wind began to blow from the south. The men thought this was the chance they needed. So they pulled up the anchor and sailed along the coast of Crete, staying close to the land.

decisions.choice: having lifted: weighed anchor
decisions.reason: The verb is used without an object as a sailing term for raising the anchor, as in 27:17 of hoisting the boat.

decisions.choice: closer: close in to the shore
decisions.reason: The word is a form meaning nearer. Long ago some took it as the name of a town, Assos, but Assos lies far away in Asia Minor.

decisions.choice: a gentle south wind: a wind that suited a run west along the coast
alternatives: a wind that drove them out to sea
decisions.reason: With the wind from the south, they could follow the south coast of Crete west to Phoenix, about a day's sail.

decisions.choice: raised the anchor
decisions.reason: English needs the object, which the sailing term implies.

records.heading: The wind called Euraquilo

records.source: μετ’ οὐ πολὺ δὲ ἔβαλεν κατ’ αὐτῆς ἄνεμος τυφωνικὸς ὁ καλούμενος Εὐρακύλων·
records.gloss: After not much however rushed down from it a wind tempestuous, the being called Euraquilo.
pieces: But soon afterward a storm wind called Euraquilo, the northeaster, came rushing down off Crete.

L.14: But not long after, a tempestuous wind, the [one] called Euraquilo, rushed down from it.

R.14: But soon a very strong wind blew down from the island. It was a storm wind from the northeast, called Euraquilo.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: Euraquilo
decisions.reason: Some early manuscripts read Euraquilo, the name of a northeast wind. Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read Euroclydon, a word not otherwise known, perhaps meaning a wind that stirs up waves. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Euraquilo: a wind from the east-northeast
decisions.reason: The name joins the Greek word for the east wind with the Latin name for the north wind, a name sailors would use. Such a wind would drive the ship away from Crete to the southwest.

decisions.choice: from it: down from Crete, off its mountains
decisions.reason: The pronoun is feminine and points back to Crete, not to the ship.

decisions.choice: tempestuous: typhoon-like, a violent, whirling wind
decisions.reason: The word is related to the word for a whirlwind or hurricane.

decisions.choice: the name Euraquilo at every level, with northeaster or northeast at Balanced and Readable
decisions.reason: The text gives the wind a name; Balanced and Readable add what the name means.

records.source: συναρπασθέντος δὲ τοῦ πλοίου καὶ μὴ δυναμένου ἀντοφθαλμεῖν τῷ ἀνέμῳ ἐπιδόντες ἐφερόμεθα.
records.gloss: Having been seized then the ship and not being able to face the wind, having given way we were being driven along.
pieces: The ship was caught up in it and could not be turned into the wind, so we gave way and drifted before it.

L.15: And the ship being seized [by it] and not able to face the wind, giving way [to it] we were driven along.

R.15: The storm took hold of the ship. The ship could not turn to face into the wind. So we gave up trying and let the wind carry us along.

decisions.choice: to face the wind: to keep the bow pointed into the wind
decisions.reason: The verb means to look someone in the eye. Of a ship it means heading into the wind.

decisions.choice: giving way: giving the ship up to the wind
decisions.reason: The participle has no object; the ship is left to run before the wind.

decisions.choice: gave up trying
decisions.reason: Readable says what giving way meant for the crew.

records.source: νησίον δέ τι ὑποδραμόντες καλούμενον Καῦδα ἰσχύσαμεν μόλις περικρατεῖς γενέσθαι τῆς σκάφης, ἣν ἄραντες βοηθείαις ἐχρῶντο ὑποζωννύντες τὸ πλοῖον· φοβούμενοί τε μὴ εἰς τὴν Σύρτιν ἐκπέσωσιν, χαλάσαντες τὸ σκεῦος, οὕτως ἐφέροντο.
records.gloss: An island then certain having run under being called Cauda, we were able with difficulty control to gain of the boat, \v 17 which having hoisted, supports they were using, undergirding the ship; fearing and lest into the Syrtis they should fall, having lowered the gear, thus they were being driven along.
pieces: We ran in the lee of a small island called Cauda, and there, with great effort, we managed to secure the ship's boat.

After hoisting it aboard, the crew used ropes to brace the ship, passing them around the hull. They were afraid of being driven onto the sandbanks of the Syrtis, so they let down the sea anchor and were carried along in that way.

L.16: And running under [the lee of] a certain small island called Cauda, we were able with difficulty to get control of the boat.
L.17: Having hoisted it [up], they used supports, undergirding the ship, and fearing that they might run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and so were driven along.

R.16: We passed by the sheltered side of a small island called Cauda. There we were able to pull in the small boat that the ship towed behind it, but it was hard work.
R.17: The sailors lifted the boat up onto the ship. Then they tied ropes around the ship to hold it together. They were afraid that the wind would push the ship onto the sandbanks of the Syrtis, near Africa. So they let out a sea anchor to slow the ship down, and they let the wind carry them along.

decisions.choice: Cauda: a small island south of the western part of Crete
decisions.reason: Its lee gave a short time of shelter. Some manuscripts spell the name Clauda; the island is the same.

decisions.choice: the boat: the small boat towed behind the ship
decisions.reason: Ships towed a small boat. In a storm it could fill with water or smash against the hull, so it was hauled aboard. It appears again in 27:30-32.

decisions.choice: supports, undergirding the ship: ropes or cables passed around the hull to hold its timbers together
alternatives: cables run lengthwise from bow to stern
decisions.reason: The words are sailing terms. Ships were strengthened with cables in a storm, but how they were fitted here, under the hull or along it, is not certain.

decisions.choice: the Syrtis: the shallow waters and sandbanks off the coast of Libya
decisions.reason: Sailors feared the Syrtis, on the north coast of Africa. A northeast wind would drive the ship toward it.

decisions.choice: lowered the gear: let out a sea anchor to slow the ship
alternatives: lowered the mainsail or the yard
decisions.reason: The word means equipment. It may be a drag anchor let out to slow the drift, or the lowering of sail. Either way they tried not to be driven too far.

decisions.choice: sea anchor
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the likeliest sense, which the meaning note marks as uncertain.

decisions.choice: that the ship towed behind it; near Africa; to slow the ship down
alternatives: the boat; the Syrtis; lowered the gear
decisions.reason: Readable explains the sailing terms and the place.

records.source: σφοδρῶς δὲ χειμαζομένων ἡμῶν τῇ ἑξῆς ἐκβολὴν ἐποιοῦντο, καὶ τῇ τρίτῃ αὐτόχειρες τὴν σκευὴν τοῦ πλοίου ἔρριψαν.
records.gloss: Violently now being storm-tossed us, on the next [day] a jettison they were making, \v 19 and on the third [day] with own hands the tackle of the ship they threw [out].
pieces: The storm pounded us so fiercely that on the following day they started jettisoning the cargo.
On the third day they took the ship's spare gear and hurled it into the sea with their own hands.

L.18: And as we were being violently storm-tossed, on the next [day] they began throwing [cargo] overboard,
L.19: and on the third [day] with their own hands they threw out the tackle of the ship.

R.18: The storm hit us very hard. So the next day the sailors began to throw cargo off the ship to make it lighter.
R.19: On the third day they even threw some of the ship's equipment into the sea with their own hands.

decisions.choice: a jettison: throwing cargo overboard to lighten the ship
decisions.reason: Only part of the cargo went; the wheat was kept until 27:38.

decisions.choice: the tackle: the ship's equipment, such as spars, rigging and spare gear
decisions.reason: The word means equipment in general. What was thrown out is not stated.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "they threw"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read "we cast out". Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: with their own hands: they did it themselves, in desperation
decisions.reason: The word stresses that the crew had to throw away their own equipment.

decisions.choice: to make it lighter
decisions.reason: Readable says why they threw cargo out.

records.source: μήτε δὲ ἡλίου μήτε ἄστρων ἐπιφαινόντων ἐπὶ πλείονας ἡμέρας, χειμῶνός τε οὐκ ὀλίγου ἐπικειμένου, λοιπὸν περιῃρεῖτο ἐλπὶς πᾶσα τοῦ σῴζεσθαι ἡμᾶς.
records.gloss: Neither now sun nor stars appearing for many days, storm and not small pressing on, from then on was being taken away hope all of the being saved us.
pieces: Day after day there was no sun and no stars to be seen, and the storm kept bearing down on us with great force. In the end every hope that we would come through alive was slipping away from us.

L.20: And neither sun nor stars appearing for many days, and no small storm pressing on [us], from then on all hope of our being saved was being taken away.

R.20: For many days we could not see the sun or the stars. The storm kept blowing very hard. Finally we gave up all hope that we would survive.

decisions.choice: no sun or stars: no way to steer or know where they were
decisions.reason: Ancient sailors found their way by the sun and the stars. Without them the crew could not tell their position.

decisions.choice: no small storm: a very great storm
decisions.reason: Luke often says "no small" to mean "great" (12:18, 15:2, 19:23-24).

decisions.choice: being saved: rescued from death at sea
decisions.reason: The verb here is about staying alive, as in 27:31 and 27:43-44.

decisions.choice: was being taken away: hope was slowly lost
decisions.reason: The tense pictures hope giving way little by little.

decisions.choice: survive
decisions.reason: Readable says what being saved meant here, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: Πολλῆς τε ἀσιτίας ὑπαρχούσης τότε σταθεὶς ὁ Παῦλος ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῶν εἶπεν· Ἔδει μέν, ὦ ἄνδρες, πειθαρχήσαντάς μοι μὴ ἀνάγεσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς Κρήτης κερδῆσαί τε τὴν ὕβριν ταύτην καὶ τὴν ζημίαν.
records.gloss: Much and going without food being, then having stood the Paul in [the] midst of them said, It was necessary indeed, O men, having obeyed me not to put to sea from the Crete and to gain the damage this and the loss.
pieces: No one had eaten for a long time. Then Paul stood up among them and said, "Men, you should have heeded me and stayed in Crete instead of setting out. You would have avoided all this damage and loss.

L.21: And when there had been long going without food, then Paul, standing in their midst, said, "O men, you should have obeyed me and not have put to sea from Crete, and [so] have been spared this damage and loss.

R.21: The men had not eaten for a long time. Then Paul stood up in front of them and said, "Men, you should have listened to me. You should not have left Crete. Then none of this damage and loss would have happened.

decisions.choice: going without food: little or no eating, not a religious fast
decisions.reason: In the storm, fear, seasickness, spoiled food and the work of saving the ship would keep people from eating (27:33).

decisions.choice: to gain this damage and loss: to be spared it
decisions.reason: To gain a loss is a Greek way of saying to escape it, by not running the risk.

decisions.choice: O men: an address to the whole ship's company
alternatives: an address to men and women
decisions.reason: The crew, the soldiers and the prisoners were men. Paul uses the same address in 27:25.

decisions.choice: you should have obeyed me: Paul recalls his warning (27:10)
decisions.reason: He recalls that his first warning came true, so that they will trust what he now says (27:22-26).

decisions.choice: stayed in Crete instead of setting out
alternatives: not put to sea from Crete
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the negative into a natural English phrase.

records.heading: Take heart

records.source: καὶ τὰ νῦν παραινῶ ὑμᾶς εὐθυμεῖν, ἀποβολὴ γὰρ ψυχῆς οὐδεμία ἔσται ἐξ ὑμῶν πλὴν τοῦ πλοίου·
records.gloss: And the now I urge you to keep up courage, loss for of life none will be from you, except of the ship.
pieces: Even so, I now urge you to take heart. Not one life among you will be lost; only the ship will go.

L.22: And now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, only of the ship.

R.22: But now I want you to take heart. None of you will die. Only the ship will be destroyed.

decisions.choice: take heart: be of good courage, stop despairing
decisions.reason: The verb means to be in good spirits. It returns in 27:25 and, as an adjective, in 27:36, when they do take heart.

decisions.choice: no loss of life: every person will survive, though the ship will not
decisions.reason: This corrects Paul's own warning in 27:10, which spoke of loss of lives. The reason follows in 27:23-24.

decisions.choice: None of you will die.
alternatives: there will be no loss of life among you
decisions.reason: Readable says it in plain words.

records.source: παρέστη γάρ μοι ταύτῃ τῇ νυκτὶ τοῦ θεοῦ, οὗ εἰμι, ᾧ καὶ λατρεύω, ἄγγελος λέγων· Μὴ φοβοῦ, Παῦλε· Καίσαρί σε δεῖ παραστῆναι, καὶ ἰδοὺ κεχάρισταί σοι ὁ θεὸς πάντας τοὺς πλέοντας μετὰ σοῦ.
records.gloss: Stood by for me this the night of the God whose I am, whom also I serve, an angel, \v 24 saying, Not fear, Paul, Caesar you it is necessary to stand before, and behold has granted to you the God all those sailing with you.
pieces: For during this night an angel came and stood beside me, an angel of the God whose I am and whom I worship.
He told me, 'Paul, do not be afraid. You are to appear before Caesar. And look: God has granted you everyone who is on board with you.'

L.23: For this night there stood by me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I also serve,
L.24: saying, 'Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar, and look, God has granted you all those sailing with you.'

R.23: Last night an angel from God came and stood next to me. I belong to God, and I worship {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
R.24: The angel said, 'Do not be afraid, Paul! You must go to Rome and stand before Caesar. And God has been kind to you. God will keep everyone sailing with you alive.'

decisions.choice: serve: worship, serve God in devotion
decisions.reason: The verb is used of religious service and worship (24:14, 26:7). Paul tells the pagan crew which God he means.

decisions.choice: Caesar: the Roman emperor, to whom Paul had appealed
decisions.reason: Paul appealed to Caesar in 25:11, and Festus agreed (25:12). The emperor at the time was Nero.

decisions.choice: you must: God's purpose for Paul
decisions.reason: The same word as in 23:11, where the Lord told Paul he must testify in Rome. The storm cannot stop it.

decisions.choice: has granted you: given you as a favor, kept alive for your sake
alternatives: has handed over to your authority
decisions.reason: The verb means to give freely. It may imply that Paul had prayed for those with him, but the text does not say so.

decisions.choice: go to Rome and
decisions.reason: Readable says where Caesar was.

decisions.choice: God has been kind to you. God will keep everyone sailing with you alive.
alternatives: God has granted you all those sailing with you
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the gift into two sentences and says what was given: their lives.

records.source: διὸ εὐθυμεῖτε, ἄνδρες· πιστεύω γὰρ τῷ θεῷ ὅτι οὕτως ἔσται καθ’ ὃν τρόπον λελάληταί μοι.
records.gloss: Therefore take heart, men; I believe for the God that thus it will be according to which way it has been told to me.
pieces: So take heart, men! I believe God: it will happen just the way I was told.

L.25: Therefore take heart, men, for I believe God that it will be just as it has been told me.

R.25: So take heart, men! I believe God. Everything will happen just as the angel told me.

decisions.choice: I believe God: I trust that what God said is true
decisions.reason: With the person in this case the verb means to believe what someone says, as in Romans 4:3.

decisions.choice: men: the whole ship's company, as in 27:21
decisions.reason: The hearers were crew, soldiers and prisoners.

decisions.choice: the angel
decisions.reason: Readable names the speaker, from 27:23.

records.source: εἰς νῆσον δέ τινα δεῖ ἡμᾶς ἐκπεσεῖν.
records.gloss: On an island however certain it is necessary us to run aground.
pieces: But we have to be cast ashore on some island."

L.26: But we must run aground on a certain island."

R.26: But our ship must be wrecked on an island."

decisions.choice: must: part of what God has said will happen
decisions.reason: The same word as in 27:24: the angel's word includes how they will be saved.

decisions.choice: run aground: be driven ashore
decisions.reason: The same verb as in 27:17 and 27:29, a sailing term for being driven onto land. It came true in 27:41.

decisions.choice: be wrecked
decisions.reason: Readable says what running aground meant for the ship.

records.source: Ὡς δὲ τεσσαρεσκαιδεκάτη νὺξ ἐγένετο διαφερομένων ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ Ἀδρίᾳ, κατὰ μέσον τῆς νυκτὸς ὑπενόουν οἱ ναῦται προσάγειν τινὰ αὐτοῖς χώραν.
records.gloss: When then fourteenth night came, being driven about us in the Adria, about [the] middle of the night were suspecting the sailors to be drawing near some land to them.
pieces: It was the fourteenth night, and we were drifting this way and that across the sea of Adria. Around midnight the crew started to suspect that land was coming near.

L.27: Now when the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven about in the Adria, about [the] middle of the night the sailors suspected that some land was drawing near to them.

R.27: On the fourteenth night the storm was still pushing us across the sea between Greece and Italy. About midnight the sailors began to think that the ship was getting close to land.

decisions.choice: the Adria: the open sea between Greece, Italy and Sicily, south of the Adriatic gulf
alternatives: the Adriatic Sea between Italy and the Balkans only
decisions.reason: Ancient writers gave the name to the wide central Mediterranean, not only to the narrow gulf now called the Adriatic.

decisions.choice: the fourteenth night: counted from the start of the storm
decisions.reason: The count runs from the day they left Fair Havens and the storm struck (27:13-19). Paul counts the same fourteen days in 27:33.

decisions.choice: land drawing near: the sailors' way of saying they were nearing land
decisions.reason: Sailors speak of land coming toward the ship. They may have heard breakers on a shore.

decisions.choice: the sea between Greece and Italy
decisions.reason: Readable says where the Adria was, as the meaning note explains, without a name the reader might take for the modern Adriatic.

records.source: καὶ βολίσαντες εὗρον ὀργυιὰς εἴκοσι, βραχὺ δὲ διαστήσαντες καὶ πάλιν βολίσαντες εὗρον ὀργυιὰς δεκαπέντε·
records.gloss: And having taken soundings they found fathoms twenty, a little then having gone farther and again having taken soundings they found fathoms fifteen.
pieces: They dropped a sounding line and found the water {{units:120 feet|20 fathoms}} deep. A little farther on they sounded again and found it {{units:90 feet|15 fathoms}}.

L.28: And having taken soundings, they found 20 fathoms, and having gone on a little farther and taken soundings again, they found 15 fathoms.

R.28: They let down a rope with a weight on the end to see how deep the water was. It was {{units:120 feet|20 fathoms}} deep. A little later they measured again. This time it was only {{units:90 feet|15 fathoms}} deep.

decisions.choice: fathom: the span of a man's outstretched arms, about six feet
decisions.reason: Twenty fathoms is about 120 feet, fifteen about 90 feet. The water was getting shallower quickly.

decisions.choice: taking soundings: lowering a weighted line to measure the depth
alternatives: looking at the color of the water
decisions.reason: Sailors measured depth with a lead weight on a marked line.

decisions.choice: modern measures, with fathoms as the alternative
decisions.reason: The units setting gives feet by default and the original fathoms as the alternative. Literal keeps fathoms.

decisions.choice: let down a rope with a weight on the end to see how deep the water was
decisions.reason: Readable explains the sailing term.

records.source: φοβούμενοί τε μή που κατὰ τραχεῖς τόπους ἐκπέσωμεν ἐκ πρύμνης ῥίψαντες ἀγκύρας τέσσαρας ηὔχοντο ἡμέραν γενέσθαι.
records.gloss: Fearing and lest somewhere against rough places we should run aground, out of [the] stern having thrown anchors four, they were praying day to come.
pieces: They were afraid we might strike a rocky coast somewhere, so they threw out four anchors from the stern and prayed for morning to come.

L.29: And fearing that we might run aground somewhere on rocky places, having cast four anchors out of [the] stern, they prayed for day to come.

R.29: The sailors were afraid that the ship would hit rocks. So they dropped four anchors from the back of the ship. Then they prayed for the sun to come up.

decisions.choice: anchors from the stern: to hold the ship with its bow toward the shore
decisions.reason: Anchoring from the stern stopped the ship swinging round and left it pointing toward land, ready to be run ashore bow first (27:40-41).

decisions.choice: prayed: prayed, or longed, for daylight
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to pray or to wish. Among frightened sailors either fits; the pagan crew would pray to their own gods.

decisions.choice: we might run aground: the narrator shares the danger
decisions.reason: The verb is first person: the fear was for all on board.

decisions.choice: the back of the ship
decisions.reason: Readable uses plain words for parts of the ship.

records.source: τῶν δὲ ναυτῶν ζητούντων φυγεῖν ἐκ τοῦ πλοίου καὶ χαλασάντων τὴν σκάφην εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν προφάσει ὡς ἐκ πρῴρης ἀγκύρας μελλόντων ἐκτείνειν, εἶπεν ὁ Παῦλος τῷ ἑκατοντάρχῃ καὶ τοῖς στρατιώταις· Ἐὰν μὴ οὗτοι μείνωσιν ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ, ὑμεῖς σωθῆναι οὐ δύνασθε.
records.gloss: Of the then sailors seeking to flee out of the ship and having lowered the boat into the sea under pretense as from [the] bow anchors being about to stretch out, \v 31 said the Paul to the centurion and to the soldiers, If not these remain in the ship, you to be saved not are able.
pieces: Meanwhile the sailors were trying to abandon the ship. They had lowered the boat into the sea on the excuse that they were about to run out anchors from the bow.
But Paul told the centurion and the soldiers, "If these men do not stay on board, there is no way for you to be saved."

L.30: And as the sailors were seeking to flee from the ship and had lowered the boat into the sea under pretense of being about to run out anchors from [the] bow,
L.31: Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, "Unless these [men] remain in the ship, you cannot be saved."

R.30: The sailors wanted to escape from the ship. They let the small boat down into the water. They pretended that they were going to put out anchors from the front of the ship.
R.31: But Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, "These sailors must stay on the ship. If they do not, you cannot be saved."

decisions.choice: the sailors' plan: to escape in the boat and leave the others
decisions.reason: Luke says the anchors were a pretense. With the sailors gone, no one would be left to handle the ship.

decisions.choice: God's promise does not set aside human means
decisions.reason: God had promised all their lives (27:24), yet Paul says they cannot be saved unless the sailors stay. The promise is kept through the crew bringing the ship in.

decisions.choice: saved: kept alive, brought safely through
decisions.reason: As in 27:20, the verb is about rescue from the sea.

decisions.choice: These sailors must stay on the ship. If they do not, you cannot be saved.
alternatives: Unless these remain in the ship, you cannot be saved.
decisions.reason: Readable splits the condition into two short sentences.

records.source: τότε ἀπέκοψαν οἱ στρατιῶται τὰ σχοινία τῆς σκάφης καὶ εἴασαν αὐτὴν ἐκπεσεῖν.
records.gloss: Then cut away the soldiers the ropes of the boat and let it fall away.
pieces: So the soldiers slashed the ropes of the boat and let it go.

L.32: Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat and let it fall away.

R.32: So the soldiers cut the ropes of the small boat. They let it fall into the sea and float away.

decisions.choice: then: the soldiers act on Paul's word
decisions.reason: The centurion now listens to Paul, as he did not in 27:11.

decisions.choice: cutting the boat loose: no one could now leave the ship except by reaching shore
alternatives: a way to save the boat
decisions.reason: Without the boat, everyone depended on the ship coming in to land (27:39-44).

records.source: Ἄχρι δὲ οὗ ἡμέρα ἤμελλεν γίνεσθαι παρεκάλει ὁ Παῦλος ἅπαντας μεταλαβεῖν τροφῆς λέγων· Τεσσαρεσκαιδεκάτην σήμερον ἡμέραν προσδοκῶντες ἄσιτοι διατελεῖτε, μηθὲν προσλαβόμενοι·
records.gloss: Until then that day was about to come, was urging the Paul all to partake of food, saying, Fourteenth today day waiting without food you continue, nothing having taken.
pieces: While they waited for daybreak, Paul kept encouraging all of them to take some food. "This is the fourteenth day," he said, "that you have kept watch without eating, taking nothing at all.

L.33: And until day was about to come, Paul was urging [them] all to take food, saying, "Today [is the] fourteenth day that you continue waiting without food, having taken nothing.

R.33: Before the sun came up, Paul told everyone to eat something. He said, "For fourteen days you have been waiting and worrying. You have not eaten anything.

decisions.choice: was urging: Paul kept on urging them
decisions.reason: The tense suggests he went on encouraging them until they ate.

decisions.choice: waiting: watching anxiously for what would happen
decisions.reason: The verb means to wait in expectation, here in suspense and fear.

decisions.choice: without food, having taken nothing: no proper meals for the whole time
alternatives: not a crumb in fourteen days
decisions.reason: Paul speaks in a strong, general way. They had hardly eaten (27:21).

decisions.choice: waiting and worrying
decisions.reason: Readable says what kind of waiting it was, as the meaning note explains.

records.heading: Bread before daybreak

records.source: διὸ παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς μεταλαβεῖν τροφῆς, τοῦτο γὰρ πρὸς τῆς ὑμετέρας σωτηρίας ὑπάρχει· οὐδενὸς γὰρ ὑμῶν θρὶξ ἀπὸ τῆς κεφαλῆς ἀπολεῖται.
records.gloss: Therefore I urge you to take of food, this for for the your survival is; of not one for of you a hair from the head will perish.
pieces: So I urge you to take some food. It is for your own survival, since not a hair on the head of any of you will be lost."

L.34: Therefore I urge you to take food, for this is for your survival; for not a hair from the head of any of you will perish."

R.34: So please eat some food. You need it to stay alive. God will keep all of you safe. Not one hair on your heads will be harmed."

decisions.choice: survival: being kept alive through the danger
decisions.reason: The noun often means salvation, but here it is about coming through the storm alive, as with the verb in 27:20 and 27:31. Food gives them strength for what lies ahead.

decisions.choice: not a hair will perish: they will be kept completely safe
decisions.reason: A saying for complete safety (1 Samuel 14:45; Luke 21:18).

decisions.choice: for: the reason they can eat with confidence
decisions.reason: They are to eat because God has promised their lives (27:24).

decisions.choice: God will keep all of you safe.
decisions.reason: Readable says what the saying about hair means and whose promise stands behind it (27:24).

records.source: εἴπας δὲ ταῦτα καὶ λαβὼν ἄρτον εὐχαρίστησεν τῷ θεῷ ἐνώπιον πάντων καὶ κλάσας ἤρξατο ἐσθίειν.
records.gloss: Having said now these things and having taken bread, he gave thanks to the God before all and having broken began to eat.
pieces: When he had said this, Paul took bread and, with everyone watching, thanked God for it. Then he broke it and started eating.

L.35: And having said these things and having taken bread, he gave thanks to God in the presence of all, and having broken [it], he began to eat.

R.35: After Paul said this, he took some bread. He thanked God for it in front of everyone. Then he broke off a piece and began to eat.

decisions.choice: took bread, gave thanks, broke it: the words of Jesus's meals
decisions.reason: The same steps appear at the feeding of the crowd (Luke 9:16), the Last Supper (Luke 22:19) and at Emmaus (Luke 24:30). Here it is an ordinary meal shared with a mostly pagan crew, but the words recall those meals.

decisions.choice: gave thanks to God: the Jewish custom of blessing God before eating
decisions.reason: Jews gave thanks to God before a meal. Paul does it openly, before all.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "began to eat"
alternatives: a few manuscripts add "giving also to us"
decisions.reason: A few manuscripts of the Western text add that Paul also gave some to his companions. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Paul
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker.

records.source: εὔθυμοι δὲ γενόμενοι πάντες καὶ αὐτοὶ προσελάβοντο τροφῆς.
records.gloss: Encouraged then having become all, also they took food.
pieces: Everyone was cheered by this, and they too took some food.

L.36: And all became encouraged, and they too took food.

R.36: This gave everyone courage, and they ate some food too.

decisions.choice: encouraged: of good courage, the same root as take heart
decisions.reason: The word picks up 27:22 and 27:25: what Paul urged has happened.

decisions.choice: they too: following Paul's example
decisions.reason: All of them took heart, and they ate as he had.

records.source: ἤμεθα δὲ αἱ πᾶσαι ψυχαὶ ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ διακόσιαι ἑβδομήκοντα ἕξ.
records.gloss: We were then the all souls in the ship two hundred seventy six.
pieces: There were 276 of us on the ship in all.

L.37: And we, all the souls in the ship, were 276.

R.37: There were 276 people on the ship, counting all of us.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: 276
decisions.reason: Codex Vaticanus reads "about seventy-six". In Greek numerals the two readings differ by a single letter, so one may have come from the other by a copying error. Most manuscripts read 276. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: souls: persons, people
decisions.reason: As in 2:41 and 7:14, souls counts people.

decisions.choice: 276: a large ship
decisions.reason: Josephus says the ship he sailed to Rome on carried about six hundred people (Life 15), so a grain ship could hold this many.

decisions.choice: of us
decisions.reason: English counts people with "of us"; the meaning note explains souls.

records.source: κορεσθέντες δὲ τροφῆς ἐκούφιζον τὸ πλοῖον ἐκβαλλόμενοι τὸν σῖτον εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν.
records.gloss: Having been filled then with food, they were lightening the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea.
pieces: Once everyone had eaten enough, they threw the wheat overboard to lighten the ship.

L.38: And having been satisfied with food, they lightened the ship, throwing the wheat out into the sea.

R.38: After everyone had eaten all they wanted, the men threw the wheat into the sea. This made the ship lighter.

decisions.choice: the wheat: the ship's cargo of grain from Egypt
alternatives: only the food supplies on board
decisions.reason: An Alexandrian ship bound for Italy (27:6) most likely carried wheat for Rome. Some take this as the remaining provisions, since part of the cargo went overboard earlier (27:18).

decisions.choice: lightening the ship: so that it would ride higher and come closer to shore
alternatives: to keep it from sinking only
decisions.reason: A lighter ship draws less water and can be run farther up a beach (27:39).

records.source: Ὅτε δὲ ἡμέρα ἐγένετο, τὴν γῆν οὐκ ἐπεγίνωσκον, κόλπον δέ τινα κατενόουν ἔχοντα αἰγιαλὸν εἰς ὃν ἐβουλεύοντο εἰ δύναιντο ἐξῶσαι τὸ πλοῖον.
records.gloss: When now day came, the land not they were recognizing; a bay however certain they were noticing having a beach, onto which they were planning if they might be able to drive out the ship.
pieces: At daybreak the land was unfamiliar to them. But they caught sight of an inlet with a beach, and they made up their minds to drive the ship onto it if possible.

L.39: And when day came, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a certain bay having a beach, onto which they planned, if they could, to drive the ship.

R.39: When the sun came up, the sailors did not know what land they had come to. But they saw a bay with a beach. They decided to try to run the ship onto the beach.

decisions.choice: beach: a smooth shore where a ship could be run aground
decisions.reason: The word means a shore or strand, here one where a ship might land safely.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "to drive out" the ship onto it
decisions.reason: Some early manuscripts have a verb that differs by one letter, meaning to bring safely to shore. The sense is close. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the land: an island they did not know, named in 28:1
decisions.reason: They learn the island's name only after they are ashore (28:1).

records.heading: All brought safely to land

records.source: καὶ τὰς ἀγκύρας περιελόντες εἴων εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν, ἅμα ἀνέντες τὰς ζευκτηρίας τῶν πηδαλίων, καὶ ἐπάραντες τὸν ἀρτέμωνα τῇ πνεούσῃ κατεῖχον εἰς τὸν αἰγιαλόν.
records.gloss: And the anchors having cast off they were leaving in the sea, at the same time having loosened the lashings of the rudders, and having raised the foresail to the blowing [wind] they were making for the beach.
pieces: They slipped the anchors and let them go into the sea, and at the same time they freed the lashings on the steering oars. Then they set the small front sail to catch the wind and steered toward the beach.

L.40: And having cast off the anchors, they left [them] in the sea, at the same time loosening the lashings of the rudders, and having hoisted the foresail to the wind, they made for the beach.

R.40: The sailors cut the ropes to the anchors and left the anchors in the sea. They also untied the ropes that held the steering paddles. Then they raised the small sail at the front of the ship, so that the wind would push it, and they headed for the beach.

decisions.choice: cast off: cut loose the anchors and let them go
decisions.reason: The verb means to take away from around. With "left them in the sea" it means the anchor cables were cut or let go.

decisions.choice: rudders: two large steering oars at the stern, one on each side
alternatives: a single rudder behind the ship
decisions.reason: Ancient ships steered with two oars. While at anchor they were lashed up out of the water; now they were let down to steer.

decisions.choice: foresail: a small sail at the bow
decisions.reason: The word is a rare sailing term. It most likely means a small sail near the bow used for steering, but its exact form is not certain.

decisions.choice: steering oars, steering paddles; the small front sail
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable describe the parts of an ancient ship, as the meaning notes explain.

records.source: περιπεσόντες δὲ εἰς τόπον διθάλασσον ἐπέκειλαν τὴν ναῦν, καὶ ἡ μὲν πρῷρα ἐρείσασα ἔμεινεν ἀσάλευτος, ἡ δὲ πρύμνα ἐλύετο ὑπὸ τῆς βίας.
records.gloss: Having fallen however into a place between two seas, they ran aground the vessel, and the indeed bow having stuck fast remained immovable, the but stern was being broken up by the force.
pieces: But they came upon a place where two seas met and ran the vessel aground. Its bow dug in and held, unable to move, while the stern began to break apart under the violence of the waves.

L.41: But falling into a place between two seas, they ran the vessel aground; and the bow, having stuck fast, remained immovable, but the stern was being broken up by the force [of the waves].

R.41: But the ship hit a sandbank where two currents of water met. The front of the ship got stuck and could not move. The back of the ship began to break apart because the waves were pounding it so hard.

decisions.choice: a place between two seas: a bank or reef where two currents met
alternatives: a narrow channel between the island and a small islet
a point of land with sea on both sides
decisions.reason: The word means having sea on both sides. It may be a sandbar or reef with water on either side, or a channel. The ship struck it before reaching the beach.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "by the force"
alternatives: many manuscripts read "by the force of the waves"
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add "of the waves". The sense is the same. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the bow stuck, the stern broke up: a contrast between the two ends of the ship
alternatives: the whole ship broke at once
decisions.reason: The Greek sets the two clauses side by side: the front was held fast, the back was being pounded apart.

decisions.choice: of the waves
decisions.reason: The force is the surf; Literal brackets the words.

records.source: τῶν δὲ στρατιωτῶν βουλὴ ἐγένετο ἵνα τοὺς δεσμώτας ἀποκτείνωσιν, μή τις ἐκκολυμβήσας διαφύγῃ·
records.gloss: Of the then soldiers plan was that the prisoners they should kill, lest anyone having swum away should escape.
pieces: The soldiers meant to kill the prisoners, so that none of them could swim off and get away.

L.42: And the soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest anyone swim away and escape.

R.42: The soldiers wanted to kill the prisoners. They did not want any of them to swim away and escape.

decisions.choice: guards answered for their prisoners with their own lives
decisions.reason: Herod put to death the guards from whom Peter escaped (12:19), and the jailer at Philippi was ready to kill himself (16:27).

decisions.choice: that they should kill ... lest anyone escape: the purpose of the plan
decisions.reason: The second clause gives the reason for the first.

records.source: ὁ δὲ ἑκατοντάρχης βουλόμενος διασῶσαι τὸν Παῦλον ἐκώλυσεν αὐτοὺς τοῦ βουλήματος, ἐκέλευσέν τε τοὺς δυναμένους κολυμβᾶν ἀπορίψαντας πρώτους ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν ἐξιέναι, καὶ τοὺς λοιποὺς οὓς μὲν ἐπὶ σανίσιν οὓς δὲ ἐπί τινων τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ πλοίου· καὶ οὕτως ἐγένετο πάντας διασωθῆναι ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν.
records.gloss: The but centurion wanting to bring safely through the Paul prevented them of the purpose, commanded and those being able to swim, having thrown [themselves] off first, onto the land to go out, \v 44 and the rest, some indeed on planks, some then on some of the things from the ship. And thus it came about all to be brought safely to the land.
pieces: The centurion, however, was determined to bring Paul through alive, and he held them back from what they meant to do. He told everyone who could swim to throw themselves into the sea first and head for the shore,
and the rest to come after them, some on boards and others on wreckage from the ship. So it was that all of them came safely to land.

L.43: But the centurion, wanting to bring Paul safely through, kept them from [their] purpose, and he ordered those able to swim to throw [themselves] overboard first [and] get to land,
L.44: and the rest [to follow], some on planks and some on [pieces] of the things from the ship. And so it came about that all were brought safely to land.

R.43: But the centurion wanted to save Paul's life. So he did not let the soldiers kill the prisoners. He told everyone who could swim to jump into the sea first and swim to the shore.
R.44: The others were to hold on to boards or to pieces of the broken ship and float to shore. And that is how everyone got safely to land.

decisions.choice: wanting to bring Paul safely through: the centurion's reason
decisions.reason: Luke says the centurion acted for Paul's sake, and so all the prisoners were spared. He had treated Paul kindly from the start (27:3).

decisions.choice: some of the things from the ship: pieces of wreckage
alternatives: some of the crew from the ship, who carried them
decisions.reason: The phrase may be neuter, things from the ship, or masculine, people from the ship who helped them. Pieces of the ship fits the planks just named.

decisions.choice: all were brought safely to land: God's promise kept
decisions.reason: The same verb as in 27:43 sums up what the angel said (27:22, 27:24) and Paul repeated (27:34).

decisions.choice: hold on to; float to shore
alternatives: on planks; on the things from the ship
decisions.reason: Readable says how the planks and wreckage were used.

decisions.choice: he did not let the soldiers kill the prisoners
alternatives: he kept them from their purpose
decisions.reason: Readable names the purpose, from 27:42.
